Failure of PDS 
* 174.   SHRI K. RAMA MOHANA RAO: 
SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIRIGIREDDY: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER  AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that PDS is a failure in the country; 
(b) if so, the reasons for such failure and the steps taken by Government 
to improve the system; 
(c) whether Government propose to introduce income generating schemes 
for poor in place of PDS; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF CONSUMER AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHANTA KUMAR): (a) and (b) No, Sir. The Public 
Distribution system (PDS) is one of the important elements of the Government's 
food security system in the country. 
The PDS is the joint responsibility of the Central Government and the 
State Govemments/UT Administrations. The Central Government is responsible 
for procuring, storing and transporting PDS commodities upto the central 
godowns and making them available to the States/UTs. Actual distribution of 
PDS commodities through Fair Price Shops  is the responsibility of the State 
Govemments/UT Administrations. 
Some shortcomings in a vast system of public distribution of subsidized 
commodities cannot be ruled out altogether. In order to make the PDS more * 
effective, efficient and accountable, th e Government has issued the Public 
Distribution System (Control) Order, 2001 under section 3 of the Essential 
Commodities Act, 1955. The salient features of the Order relate to proper 
identification of eligible families, issue of ration cards, licensing of fair price 
shops, scale of issue and issue prices, distribution of essential commodities and 
monitoring. Any contravention of the provisions of clauses 3,4,6 and 7 of the 
Order is liable for criminal punishment under section 7 of the Essential 
Commodities Act, 1955. 
The Government has advised the State Govemments/UT Administrations 
to involve the Gram Panchayats more substantially in the supervision and 
monitoring of the PDS, especially at the FPS level, as a measure of social 
34 

[29 November, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
audit. A Model Citizens' Charter has also been drawn and circulated to States/ 
UTs for adoption. 
(c) and (d) No such proposal to cep lace the PDS is under consideration 
at present. However, the Government has launched many schemes, including 
employment generating schemes, for the welfare of the poor.

Statement-I 
Guidelines on organisational restructuring of FCI  
To tackle the problem of acute stagnation among the employees of the 
Corporation, the Government of India has issued broad guidelines on 20.4.2000 
to Food Corporation of India on organisational restructuring with specific 
reference to manpower management, cadre management and Career 
progression. The salient features of the guidelines are as under— 
(i)   Rationalisation of depots and manning of depots by Assistant 
Managers (depot) and above 
(ii)   Revision of norms through independent outside agency 
(iii)   Creation of Litigation Cells and Computer Cells 
(iv)   Revamping of Quality Control Machinery

(v)   Watch & Ward staff deployment 
(vi)   Upgrading the existing posts 
(vii)   Induction of 100 management trainees every year. 
(viii)   Shiffng of sanctions of surplus staff to the needy places within Zone 
and outside Zone 
(ix)   Maintaining the existing panpower 
(x)   Winding up of port operations and tackling the problems of past 
workers. 
(xi)   Tackling labour problems.

The management had been contemplating the measures to tone up the 
administration meeting to the challenge of the current scenario, it was felt 
essential that there should be more decentralisation of authority and powers 
and consequently the depots are managed at least by Assistant Manager. 
Similarly, there would be need for restructuring the set up at the districts. 
On the other hand, the unions had been raising demand for removal of 
acute stagnation of the employees in th e same post for a long time alongwith 
the demand for removal of disparity in careers prospects among employees 
belonging to different grades/cadres/zones. The management felt a need for 
organisational restructure with the reasonable opportunity of at least 3 
promotions to every employee in category III level i.e. upto the level of 
Assistant manager if the employees are to be suitably motivated to take up the 
challenge of the organisational restructure. However, it may not be possible 
to; ensure the same to the existing employees as many employees could not 
get any promotion in the service career so far and have been left with a very 
limited service of 5 to 10 years. Hence only younger employees with longer 
service would reasonably anticipate su ch a career progressi on alongwith the 
future new recruits. 
To mitigate the hardship and to en sure the existing employees having 
sufficient service have career progression, a scheme of organisational 
restructure alongwith cadre restruct ure was discussed with the various 
recognised unions under different spells and after protracted negotiations held 
between the management and the FCEESU the following understanding has 
been reached in full and final settlement of the dmand in respect of the said 
matter of stagnation. A formal settlement would be signed with the union on 
receipt of the approval of the Government  of india to the proposals contained 
in the Memorandum of Understanding and the settlement would be on receipt

TERMS OF UNDERSTANDING 
1. STAFF NORMS 
1.1 Both the management and the union had agreed that there was a 
need for a thorough review of the existing norms consequent to the changes in 
the nature of operations as well as the need for modernisation and that the task 
of framing fresh norms for staff sanctions would be entrusted to an independent 
out side agency who would interact with the management as well as unions 
before framing the fresh norms. 
1.2 The norms would be comprehensive covering all the areas of 
operations presently undertaken by the Corporation. It would in turn keep in 
view the.following material changes. 
i) The Corporation would switch over to a single cadre system except 
in case of Engineering cadre as far as unionised, employees are 
concerned. The new recruits would be given on the job training at 
entry level and they shall discharge all duties as may be assigned 
from time to time without an y job distinction like quality 
maintenance, stock holding, maintenance of accounts, etc. 
ii) The career advancement would be so provided as to enable any 
unionised employees in Scale No. 5 in category III to reach the 
level of Assistant Manager befor superanuation. in case of category 
IV employees suitable career advancement proposal would be 
available for them to reach atleas t the first level of category HI 
post. 
iii) The recruitment an filling up policy would also be so worked out as 
to enable and ensured career advancement alongwith proviso for 
accelerate4 promotion through departmental test. The intake points 
would be cmically reviewed to avoid lateral entry at all stages. 
iv) There would be inbuilt proviso for a compulsory periodical review 
of sanctions once in 5 years in consultation with the unions. This 
would be in addition to the usual proviso for creation of new post/ 
aboliton of old post as per operational need defind therein.

Diversion of PDS foodgrains 
1233. SHRI R.P. GOENKA: Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS, 
FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
94 

[29 November, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(a) whether the Planning Commission has, in a detailed study, highlighted 
the evil of diversion of PDS grains and other stocks to the black market; 
(b) if so, the relevant findings of the study; 
(c) whether it is a fact that 31 per cent rice, 36 per cent wheat and 23 per 
cent sugar have been diverted so far; 
(d) if so, the assessment of the loss to the national exchequer; and 
(e) the steps being taken to plug this diversion? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI ASHOK 
PRADHAN): (a) to (d) Planning Commission has not conducted any 
independent study on diversion from PDS. However, in the Mid-Term Appraisal 
of Ninth Five Year Plan (1997—2002), the Planning Commission has stated 
that all is not well with PDS in India. Based on a study conducted by the Tata 
Economic Consultancy Services (TECS) in 1997, the Planning Commission 
has stated that there is 36% diversio n of wheat, 31% diversion of rice and 
23% diversion of sugar from the system at the national level. 
The percentage of diversion with reference to different target groups for 
whom there are different Central Issue Prices is not available from the study 
which was conducted around the time targeted PDS was introduced. The 
findings were based on a sample of beneficiaries selected for the study. It is, 
therefore, not possible to quantify the loss of subsidy in monetary terms. 
(e) The Public Distribution System is implemented under the joint 
responsibility of the Central and State Govemments/UT Administrations. The 
Central Government is responsible for procurement, storage and transportation 
of the PDS commodities upto the central godowns and making them available 
to the States. The responsibility for distribution to the consumers through the 
Fair Price Shops and administration of the PDS rests with the State Governments 
and UT Administrations. State Governments have been requested to closely 
monitor PDS at the Fair Price Shops (FPS) and other levels and to make 
arrangement for distribution of PDS commodities in a transparent and 
accountable manner by involvement of Panchayati Raj Institutions (PRls). 
In order the streamline the functioning of Public Distribution System 
(PDS) and make it more accountable and e ffective, Govt, of India has issued 
the Public Distribution System (Control) Order, 2001 under Sector 3 of the 
Essential Commodities Act, 1955. The provisions of the PDS (Control) 
95 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2001 ] 
Order, 2001 can be used by the State Govemments/UT Administrations to 
remedy the Public Distribution System and make it transparent and accountable. 
States/UTs have also been asked to eliminate bogus ration cards and initiate 
action against erring FPS owners unde r Section 3 of Essential Commodities 
Act, 1955.

the system? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS, FOOD AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI ASHOK 
PRADHAN): (a) and (b) in order to streamline the functioning of Public 
Distribution System (PDS) and make it more accountable and effective, 
Government of India has issued the Public Distribution System (Control) Order 
2001 under Section 3 of Essential Commodities Act, 1955. This order contains 
provisions in regard to the following matters:— 
(i) Identification of families living below the poverty line; 
(ii) Ration cards; 
(iii) Scale and Issue prices; 
(iv) Distribution of foodgrains; 
(v) Licensing; 
(vi) Monitoring; and 
(vii) Penalities for violation 
(c) The provisions of the PDS (Control) Order, 2001 can be used by the 
State Govemment/UT Administrations to remedy the Public Distribution 
System and make it transparent and accountable. Contraventions of the 
provisions of the orders is a cognizable offence under Section 3 of E.C. Act, 
1955. It is hoped that it will help to reduce chances of malpractices.

(c) The Interim Report is under examination.

Statement 
Recommendations of the High Level Committee on long term Grain Policy, 
in its Interim Report 
I. Recommendations for immediate-run 
(1) Statutory levies imposed on purchase of foodgrains amount to as 
much as 12.5 per cent of the pr ocurement price in certain States. 
The Committee recognizes that pa yments by the FCI as statutory 
levies to State Governments are essentially transfers from the 
Centre to State Governments and should be counted as such. It 
therefore recommends the elimination of such levies on foodgrain, 
an essential commodity. Till such time, the statutory levies charged 
by States should be settled separately between the Centre and the 
State Governments without involving FCI or its economic cost. 
This would require necessary amendments in the States Sales 
Tax Acts. Alternatively, the amounts being implicitly transferred 
to States from the Central Government in the form of statutory 
levies may be transferred directly in the form of current transfers. 
(2) The Committee notes with concern attempts by various producing 
State Governments to have the quality norms for purchase of food-
grain for the Central pool relaxed from time to time. Many 
consuming State Governments have refused to accept such food-
grains for PDS distribution. The Committee therefore recommends 
that FAQ norms to be strictly adhered to. If any State Government 
requests for relaxation of quality norms, this should be invariably 
accompanied by an appropriate price reduction besides exemption 
from statutory State levies. 
(3) The MSP for paddy and the levy price for rice be fixed only for a 
single grade, as against Common and Grade 'A' at present. 
110 

[29 November, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
(4) OMSS prices should cover not only the acquisition cost but also, 
as far as possible, reflect fully the differences in costs of transport 
and storage at different points of sale. This should be at least FCI's 
acquisition cost less statutory levies. Further, differentials across 
regions should be restored, and there should be a pre-announced 
graded escalation per quarter. 
(5) In order to revive the offtake from PDS system, the APL population 
needs to brought into the net by reducing the APL price to 80% of 
the economic cost, excluding statutory levies or about 75% of the 
present economic cost including levies. The BPL price should be 
50% of the economic cost, excluding the statutory levies. This 
would help improve the viability of the distribution network and 
thus improve BPL offtake as well. 
(6) For the BPL families, the quota should depend on the number of 
members in a family. The Committee recommends that each BPL 
family be permitted to purchase up to 5 kg per person at the 
announced BPL price per month or an allocation of 20 kg per 
family whichever is higher. Any additional requirement may be 
provided at the APL price. 
(7) For the areas covered earlier und er the Revamped PDS (1775 
blocks), and areas currently drought affected or ravaged by other 
natural calamity like floods, cyclones, earthquakes, etc., a universal 
PDS be introduced at BPL prices and quota. 
(8) In the Revamped PDS areas, the Supplementary Nutrition 
Programme (SNP) of ICDS may be strengthened. Similarly, the 
Mid-day Meal Scheme could be strengthened by extending its 
coverage to secondary school students. 
(9) The Committee strongly urges the Government to examine ways 
of expanding programmes of employment generation to create an 
effective demand for foodgrains. 
(i) Ideally, a massive food for work type programs should be 
launched. The primary responsibility of launching these 
programs should rest with Ministry of Rural Development. 
(ii) There may however be practical implementation problems in 
making payments in kind. In these cases, employment 
111 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2001 ] 
provisions with wage payments in cash may be increased 
simultaneously with an expansion in PDS supplies and 
strengthening of PDS network. 
(iii) The existing restriction on employment in the Employment 
Assurance Scheme (EAS) to BPL cardholders alone should 
be removed immediately. 
To facilitate speedier implementation of food for work schemes, an 
interim allocation of 2 to 3 million tonnes of foodgrains may be made available 
to the States at discounted BPL pri ce. The main objective should be to 
supplement/amplify schemes currently undertaken by the States such as PM's 
Sarak Rozgar Yojana. 
II. Recommendations for Long-run 
(1) The MSP should be announced before the sowing season on the 
basis of C2 cost of production (i.e., all costs including the imputed 
costs of family labour, owned capital, and rental on owned land) 
on the recommendations of the CACP. At this price the Central 
Government should undertake open ended purchase of FAQ of 
grains to assure growers an adequate return on their cost. 
(2) The Central Government may purchase above MSP in situations 
where market conditions warrant to make up any shortages in 
normative buffer stocks and to meet PDS requirements. This price 
should be determined by the FCI on the basis of market assessment 
in each year. And this should not from the basis of MSP for the 
next year. 
(3) The Central Government should instruct its procuring agencies/ 
State Governments to extend their MSP operations more effectively 
to States/regions, such as Assam, Bihar, Orissa and Uttar Pradesh, 
where farmers have reported to have been receiving prices below 
MSP. 
(4) There is a need for immediate action to reduce taxation on essential 
food items and to minimize barriers to private trade. 
(5) OMSS should not distort markets by selling grains at heavily 
subsidized prices. The minimum price for OMSS should not be 
below the acquisition cost of FCI less statutory levies with additions 
for transport and storage costs in different regions and at different 
times of the year. 
112 

[29 November, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(6) System of exports and imports of foodgrains should be based on a 
system of variable tariffs which should replace quotas. This is 
required for stabilization of prices  in an open economy. Also, as 
far as possible, releases for exports from public stocks should be 
on best commercial terms. 
(7) Decentralisation of the foodgrain  procurement and distribution 
system is desirable provided this is seen as a means by which 
States which can be given greater flexibility in design of their 
PDS and the FCI be given greater incentive for cost control, without 
the Central Government diluting its commitment to the 
requirements of price stabilization and food security. 
(8) In principle, the Committee believes that dual/multiple prices of 
the PDS are distortionary and provide scope for leakage. 
(9) The basic approach of the Committee is that barriers to trade in 
the grain market should be removed so as to make it more integrated 
nationally. The role of public intervention should primarily be to 
stabilize prices and that any system  of price stabilization must be 
national in scope. Also, decentra lization will be acceptable to the 
States only if this is carried out in a manner which does not involve 
the Centre passing on to them the fiscal costs that it bears currently. 
The Committee will elaborate on the above mentioned issues in 
its final report.

1254. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHAR YA: Will the Minister of 
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state:

become the epicenter of terrorism, narc otics and obscurantist ideologies. The 
present war in Afghanistan is fight agai nst terrorist and obscurantist forces of

all efforts aimed at eradicating this menace from this world.

118 

[ 29 November, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA

India's initiatives to fight terrorism 
1256. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHAR YA: Will the Minister of 
EXTERNAL AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the inhuman terrorism triggered US rage and its consequent 
attack on Afghanistan killing many children, women and other civilians is 
threatening to escalate a global war; 
(b) if so, whether India should immediately initiate some global actions 
to fight out terrorism of any hue and devastating war; 
(c) if so, whether some actions have already been initiated to render 
peace a chance; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT SINGH): 
(a) The military campaign in Afghanistan is in response to the terrorist attacks 
on September 11, 2001 in the USA. 
(b) to (d) The tragic events of September, 11 have brought heightened 
awareness in the international commun ity of the urgent need to combat 
terrorism. As a victim of terrorism for over two decades, India has consistently 
stressed that combating terrorism should have the highest priority on the global 
agenda. We have emphasised that terror ism is a global menace which cannot 
be compartmentalised; that the fight against it has to go beyond the immediate; 
and has to be comprehensive, global and sustained. India has also pointed out 
that there can be no justification for acts of terrorism; political, religious, 
ethnic, ideological or any oher. Intern ational measures to counter terrorism 
should encompass not only the perpetrators of terrorist acts, but also those 
who incite, support, finance or extend safe havens to terrorists. 
120 

[29 November, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
During the UN General Assembly (UNGA) session on November 10, 
2001, the Prime Minister, ShriAtal Behari Vajpayee forcefully conveyed India's 
point of view including our concerns on cross border terrorism. 
India has welcomed international efforts including efforts under the 
United Nations to counter terrorism. In  this framework, India has welcomed 
the UN Security Council Resolution 1373 of September 28, 2001. India is 
also piloting a Comprehensive Convention on International Terrorism (CCIT) 
to strengthen the legal framework for countering terrorism. At the United 
Nations discussions on CCIT are continuing. 
India supports the efforts being made by the international community, 
including through the UN, for the earl y return of peace and normalcy in 
Afghanistan.

Statement 
Incentives for Software Sector 
1. Export Promotion Capital Goods scheme (EPCG) has been 
rationalised and extended uniformly to all sectors without any 
threshold limit on payment of 5% duty. 
2. Approvals for all foreign direct investment proposals relating to the 
Information Technology sector, with the exception of Business-to-
Consumer (B2C) e-commerce are under the automatic route. 
3. Software Technology Parks (STP) Scheme is implemented under the 
aegis of the Ministry of Information Technology through a single 
window mechanism of the Inter-Ministerial Standing Committee 
(IMSC). 
4. Accelerated depreciation norms for computers and computer 
peripherals for units under Export Oriented schemes (EOU/EP27 
STP/EHTP) have been enhanced. These shall stand depreciated to overall 
limit of 90% over a period of 3 years instead of around 5 years earlier. 
151 

RAJYA SABHA [29 November, 2001 ] 
5. DTA access upto 50% of the FOB value of export is permitted for 
software units under EOU/STP schemes. 
6. In the 2000-01 Budget, Customs duty on Computers and 
Peripherals had been reduced from 20% to 15% and continues to 
be same. The Customs duty on all storage devices, integrated 
circuits, microprocessors, data display tubes and deflection 
components of colour monitors also continues at 0%. In the 2001-
02 Budget, Customs duty on Information Technology Agreement 
(ITA-1) items ofWTO (IT and Telecom products) has been reduced 
from existing 20-25% to 15%. 
7. Information Technology Software is exempted from Customs and 
Excise Duty. 
8. EOU/EPZ/STP/EHTP units are exempted from payment of Income 
Tax on export profits, upto 2010, in terms of Section lOAand 10B 
of the Income Tax Act. On site development of computer software 
and services will also be eligible for tax exemption. 
9. Definition of Computer Software, as in Section 80HHE of the 
Income Tax Act has been widened to include transmission of data. 
10. Benefit of Section 80 HHE is available to supporting software 
developers. 
11. Exemption of withholding tax on interest on External Commercial 
Borrowings (ECBs) has been extended to the IT sector. 
12. IT Enabled Services have been made eligible for Income Tax 
benefit under Sections 10A, 10B and 80HHE of the Income Tax 
Act. 
13. A National Venture Fund for Software and IT Industry (NFSIT) 
has been set up with a corpus of Rs. 100 crores, out of which MIT 
shall contribute Rs. 30 crores. 
14. Income by way of dividends or long-term capital gains of a Venture 
Capital Fund or Venture Capital company from investment made 
by way of equity shares in a Venture Capital Undertaking, which 
has been expanded to include the Software and IT  sectors, will 
henceforth not be included in computing the total income. 
15. To give thrust to Venture Capital finance, SEBI has been made the 
single point nodal agency for registration and regulation of both 
domestic and overseas venture capital funds. 
152 

[29 November, 2001 ] RAJYA SABHA 
16. There will be no tax on distributed or undistributed income of 
Venture Capital Funds. The income distributed by the VCFs will 
only be taxed in the hands of the investors at the rates applicable 
to the nature of the income. VCFs will continue to be eligible for 
exemption even if the shares of the VC undertaking in which the 
VCFs have made the initial investment are subsequently listed in 
a recognised stock exchange in India. 
17. Under policy on portfolio investment, Foreign Institutional 
Investors (FIIs) are permitted to invest in a company upto an 
aggregate of 24% of equity shar es, extendable upto 40% subject 
to approvals. This limit has been raised from 40% to 49% in the 
Budget 2001-02. 
18. Under the employee Stock Option Scheme, income tax payable 
on income from GDRs purchased in foreign currency by a resident 
employee of IT software and serv ice companies, shall be at a 
concessional rate of 10%. 
19. Tax holidays under provisions of Section 80-1A (Infrastructure 
Status) has been extended to Internet Service Providers (ISPs) and 
Broadband Network providers. 
20. Two-way fungibility has been permitted for ADRs/GDRs. Local 
shares can now be reconverted into ADRs/GDRs, subject to sectoral 
caps. 
21. To induce more investment for R&D activities, a weighted 
deduction of 125% on the sums paid to any university, college or 
an institution or a Scientific res earch association for the purpose 
of scientific, social or statistical research has been provided. 
22. Information Technology Act 2000 has been enacted. This act deals 
with Cyber Security, Cyber Crime and other information security 
related legal aspects. This will encourage expansion of p-commerce 
through internet.

support Centre in the USA, which is operational since November, 
1999, to promote business for STP units and provide marketing 
support to SMEs.

1319. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA: Will the Minister of LABOUR be

MUNI LAI..L): (a) A five judge Constitution Bench of the Supreme Court in 
their judgement dated 30.08.2001 in the case of Steel Authority of India Limited

affirmed that the Contract Labour (Regulation and Abolition) Act, 1970 does

Gramodaya Schemes for rural people 
1337.     PROF. M.M. AGARWAL: 
SHRI BACHANI LEKHRAJ: 
Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government have started any 'Gramodaya Scheme' to cater to the 
needs of the important sectors like availability of drinking water, housing, nutrition, 
primary health, elementary education and rural electrification in order to uplift the 
living standard in the rural areas of the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the main objective of the said scheme; 
(d) the details of the targets under the said scheme and the amount allocated 
to each State/UT; and 
186 

[29 November, 2001] RAJYA SABHA 
(e) The details of the steps being taken by Government to achieve the 
said targets in order to bring prosperity in the villages? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) Yes, Sir.In- order to achieve the 
objective of sustainable human development at the village level, the Pradhan 
Mantri Gramodaya Yojana (PMGY) has been launched by the Government 
during the Annual Plan 2000-01 in all the States and Union Territories. 
(b) There are six components under PMGY. These are Primary Health, 
Primary Education, Safe Drinking Wate r, Rural Shelter, Nutrition and Rural 
Electrification. Rural Electrification has been added as the sixth component 
under PMGY in the Annual Plan 2001-02. Under PMGY, Additional Central 
Assistance (ACA) is provided to the States and Union Territories to implement 
various components of the Programme. 
(c) The main objective of the Programme is to ensure provision of basic 
minimum services (the various components of PMGY) to all rural households 
in the country so that sustainable hu man development could be achieved at 
the village level. 
(d) The State and UT-wise allocation of ACA during the Annual Plan 
2000-01 and 2001-02 are given in Stat ement-I and Statement-II respectively 
(See below). The States and Union Territories are required to earmark at least 
10 per cent of their ACA for each of the components under PMGY except for 
Nutrition for which a minimum 15 per cent earmarking has been stipulated 
under the guidelines. This works out the 65 per cent of the total ACA which is 
mandatorily earmarked for six components of PMGY. The residual 35 per 
cent of ACA is required state to be allocated by the States and Union Territories 
as per their own discretion. 
Keeping in view the allocation for various components of PMGY, the 
States and Union Territories fix annual targets under each component. The 
proposals are sent to the concerned Central Ministries and Departments who 
in turn examine the same and make recommendation to the Ministry of Finance 
for release of ACA to the States and Union Territories. 
(e) As stipulated in the guidelines , the Annual Plan proposals under 
PMGY are required to be implemented in a time bound manner. The second 
instalment of ACA under a component of PMGY is released only after a minimum 
50 per cent expenditure is incurred and reported to the concerned Central 
Ministries and Departments. While financial and physical monitoring of PMGY 
are carried out by the concerned Central Ministries and Department;, the over 
all coordination of PMGY is the responsibility of the Planning Commission.

"The   Guru's   execution   could   not   have   been   taken   
without

anytrhg so far as

done have caused misery and damage. But we have assuaged your 
feelings by changing the history textbook. That is your last resort. You

future of the nation. What you ar e teaching today is what the nation 
will become tomorrow. Therefore, please do not do it. 
While concluding, I have to make a few demands as a 
Member of this House. No.1, you want to change the Education 
Policy. Do it; but do it if you can get the approval of Parliament. That is 
what democracy calls upon you to do. That is what the Constitution

Education Policy. Tell us in a transparent manner what you want to 
do. Get the approval of Parliament and then you do it.   If you don't get 
the approval, you cannot do it. 
Education is in the Concurrent List of our Constitution. You 
can't go over the head of the Stat e Governments, which have to 
implement the things, which have to give the money, which have to 
run the schools, which have got to do everything. You have got to do 
nothing except to give instructions. Therefore, my second demand is, 
convene immediately a meeting of the Central Advisory Board of 
Education wherein all the State

the destruction of this country. We will not compromise on this. In 
spite of what you may say, we st and, work and sacrifice for the unity 
of this country, for the democracy to prevail in this great nation.

DR. RAJA RAMANNA (Nominat ed): Thank you, Mr. Vice-
Chairman, Sir. I would like to speak on this Resolution because I feel 
that it is a very timely one. My own experience is not of a city man. I 
am the Chairman of a Task Force set up in Karnataka, specifically 
looking at the primary schools and why they are in a poor form, 
especially in the backward areas. We always judge the condition of 
education by just looking at the elite schools in Bangalore, Mysore 
and, of course, from Delhi in the North. But if you go to the village 
schools now, you will find that they are exactly in the same position 
they were during the British days.  Nothing has happened. Of course, 
we can improve the schools. I have spent my MPLADS money on 
making schools with roofs, making schools where water is available, 
where lavatories are available. If the city does not use the schools for 
other purposes, then you find that t he students recognise it as a place 
of learning. I have often noticed t hat, many a time, the school children 
come at the proper time for their studies, sit in straight lines, and I was 
delighted to see them. But when you ask, 'Where is the teacher?', you 
get a reply, "Ohl He comes only at 4 o' clock in the evening or one 
hour before the school closes." I mention this particular aspect of 
teachers not being there, because you select some teacher through 
some promotion system and he is posted at a place where he does 
not want to go and for the rest of  his life i.e., until he gets himself 
transferred, he does not take any interest in his job. So, it does not 
matter what book you give him, wh at Safronisation you do or what 
Talibanisation you do; he is a non-entity in the educational process. 
Therefore, our first duty should be to see that the teacher is educated 
and, in the process of education, he should have the discrimination to 
find out where we are over-stressing certain aspects of knowledge, 
which may give them a communal base or which may give them a 
religious base or which may give them a wrong base.   It is true that 
we

have got a very confused educational history. I myself went to one of 
the Christian schools. Yes. The books were biased. But the 
background that we had in our own house was a source of correctives 
of what was good, what was bad and what was necessary in a colonial 
system. There are many things which you can replace for bad teaching 
and I have always thought that music should be taught in the primary 
school itself. You will be surprised to know that in-the old British days, 
in all the villages, there used to be a harmonium. Every village had a 
teacher and the students got benefited. But what happened? Mr. 
Keskar I think may mention his name correctly a former Minister, under 
some very good advice said that harmonium was bad for Carnatik 
Music and should be banned. Then, it  was banned from the All India 
Radio and the general tendency was to ban the harmonium player and 
harmonium. So, you get no music at all. And, only a few days ago, I 
had put a question here, in this very  House. After much activity, I have 
got the All India Radio to recognise the solo harmonium player as a 
suitable one for performance. But he said, "Sir, yes. The All-India Radio 
has recognised, but the Doordarshan does not recognise." I asked the 
question, 'Why?' And the reply to the question is very interesting. The 
reply says, "About harmonium we cannot decide, because Prasar 
Bharati is all powerful in deciding whether harmonium is good or bad 
for schools." This is how it goes on. And we keep schools right at the 
very level where they were found, independence came. Now, what do 
we do next? It is no use simply criticising all the time I am exactly in 
the middle of the House and I do not s peak either for this side or that 
side. The basic issue is how to improve education and how to make it 
interesting. You cannot have teacher who does not take interest in his 
job. You cannot have a badly trained teacher. And, I think, all the 
systems that we have for training teachers, from my own personal 
experience, are very poor. The firs t priority should be given to the 
training of teachers. Books, pencils, papers, paintings and things like 
that come after that. A teacher must be one who creates interest. We, 
in our committees, were thinking  of introducing things like T.V., 
Internet and what the Indian Institute of Science is trying to make, a 
simputor so that teachers can get assistance by getting into direct 
contact with some other place for any problem that has to be solved. 
Many a time we find teachers who are not able to multiply two 
numbers with two numbers. That, by itself, is not a proof of anything, 
but we would expect that one who is  going to teach children should, at 
least, know multiplication tables, at the lower levels; and, of course, 
also the knowledge of computer, at a later stage.   I was very happy 
when the Minister gladly, this morning,

accepted my suggestion that, first, el ectricity should come to schools. 
Mr. Mukherjee also supported me because all the modern gadgets 
can be thought of for improving education only when electricity comes 
to schools. Also, bring it to the leve l-not subject-wise but quality-wise - 
of European schooling in the villages. In European schools you will not 
see any difference between the schools in the cities and the schools in 
the towns. Of course, they have elite schools for preparing for different 
political thoughts. Such schools also exist. We have not gone into that 
kind of democracy yet. That is a historic democracy of European 
nations. But we must modernise our education. There is no use of 
going into old-fashioned methods - one school, one teacher, forty 
children, sixty children, half a room, no water, no tap, and so on, and 
make them more like, what they call,  pens, so that they stay out of 
mischief, or, allow the parents to go  to work. I will be very happy if 
electricity comes and evening classe s take place. It will solve many 
problems. But who will solve these pr oblems? We are leaving it to the 
States, with a very large number of  schools. Unless the problem is 
divided into possible capabilities, we will remain where we are. I am 
sure illiteracy can be overcome within  two years, if everybody makes 
efforts in villages and towns, as they did in Burma. I am told that the 
Buddhist priests decided that everybody must learn to read; and within 
two years, I believe, everybody could read. However, I have not 
verified it. But it is a good enough statement. That's what happened in 
Kerela also, where Missionary and Christian schools did a lot for it. I 
don't see any reason why this cannot be imitated here. Simply 
complaining that the books are not right, this is not right, that is not 
right, will not help. I would say, if the teacher is not right, the 
atmosphere is not right, nothing c an be achieved. The attitude of the 
general public should be that they mu st keep away from illiteracy. The 
attitude that somebody else will do it, is also the cause for our decay. 
So, while bringing changes in the system, modifications in the Bill, 
amendments, must be taken into account, and we should not get lost 
into generalities.  Thank you very much.

DR. (MS.) P. SELVIE DAS (N ominated): I thank you very 
much, Mr. Vice-Chairman, Sir, for giving me an opportunity to take part 
in the discussion on the National Education Policy of 1986. 
250 

[29 November, 2001]      RAJYA SABHA 
I very much appreciated the st atement made by one of our 
hon. Members that education should make an individual human. That 
is really a wonderful statement, I felt. Education is a fundamental right 
of every child in our country. Of course, it has been realised and in 
1950 itself, a directive was given in the Constitution to provide free 
and compulsory education. Somehow, we were not able to achieve it 
even in the 10 years of time-span t hat was given. However, time and 
again, they have kept that as the go al to achieve. But, in course of 
time, we were able to achieve quantitative increase in education. The 
number of institutions in creased. Even in rural areas, at a distance of 
one kilometre, village people could reach the institution. But what type 
of institutions do we have? If we thin k in terms of qua lity, if you take 
the infrastructure in these institutions, it is not a thing that we could 
speak of. 
Our hon. Member Dr. Raja Ramanna talked about teachers, 
teachers teaching in rural areas, specially. Well, of course, we say, 
they are all trained teachers. It may be that they have the stamp of 
training, for calling themselves 't rained teachers'. But I have never 
known people having the kind of dedication, devotion, required for that 
profession. They never had the ambition to motivate the children, to 
inspire the children. I always looked up to him, Dr. Raja Ramanna. 
When, at 4 o'clock, a teacher or principal gets into the institution, what 
type of education children would be receiving? However, in 1968 
itself, when the National Policy on Education was introduced, the goal 
was to promote a sense of common citizenship and a radical re-
construction of the education system, to improve the quality at all 
stages--pre-primary, primary, elem entary, high school education and 
higher education, including university education. Of course, an 
emphasis on science and technol ogy was given in addition to 
cultivation of moral value. This has been revised naturally. From 1968 
to 1985, there was a long span of time. The scenario in our country 
has changed. Naturally, everybody, the leaders, the educationists, the 
public, felt that there is a need for  revision in the policy and it was 
thought in 1985 and brought out in 1986. When the New Policy on 
Education was brought out in 1986, I very well remember, great 
leaders, academicians, educationists, from different places, had said 
tnat it was the old wine in a new bottle. Well, they could not have 
changed the nomenclature of primar y education, the nomenclature of 
elementary education. However, due to  the criticism, a plan of action 
was worked out in 1992. 
251

4.00 P.M. 
That was really very, very clear. Particularly, what I 
appreciated and what I liked very much about the emphasis that was 
given in 1986 Policy was, about the education for women, the girl 
child. That impressed me a lot, and secondly, the education for the 
Scheduled Castes and the Scheduled Tribes, education for the 
backward people, education for the mi norities, they have spelt it out 
very clearly in the Plan of Action, and then the emphasis. What was 
started in 1968, down to 1986, they  gave greater emphasis to moral 
values or value-based education. Of course, as I said earlier, there 
have been achievements in education from 1950 onwards not only in 
urban areas but also in rural areas. Schools have been established 
quantitatively, but not qualitatively. Even to this day, I cannot compare 
a school in a rural area or a municipal school or a Government school 
with any of the public schools that we have. Some of us can really 
boast that we have studied in ve ry good schools. People who could 
afford, went to the public schools and their character was built up, 
moral values were inculcated in them, and it was good. But how about 
the majority of children in our c ountry who could not afford public 
school education and what is their fate? As far as the rural schools are 
concerned, no infrastructure is there, no social service is rendered to 
them, no benefit of trained teachers to them, and more than that, no 
dedicated teachers are there. A variety of new challenges and social 
needs made it imperative to review the policy of 1968 to 1986. Now, I 
feel, in the same way, from 1986 to this day, that is, 2001, there is a 
great need to review the same. Our society has changed 
tremendously. A number of problems have creeped in. So, it is very 
necessary that we have to change t he policy. If we have to review the 
policy now, I feel, greater emphasis should be given to value-based 
education. Well, when I talk about the value-based education, I would 
like to say that education is for life, not for living. Swami Vivekananda 
said: "Education is for life-building, man-making and character-
making." Education for life means not only for livelihood but also to 
develop oneself. In recent times, we are hearing so much about 
Bhagwan Sri Satya Sai Baba. In the past half a century, he has been 
talking about the value-based education for the development of a 
nation. He and his organization have been establishing several 
institutions not only in the country but also in different parts of the 
world. They have adopted this philosophy and they are trying to 
implement the same in their institutions. In their philosophy, emphasis 
is laid on honesty, truth and dharma. Dharma is the first step that we 
have to take. But if it is too big a terminology for us to accept,  it is 
nothing but 
252 

[29 November, 2001]      RAJYA SABHA 
righteousness, and if rightneousness, honesty and love for humanity 
are there, why are we having so many communal riots? Why are we 
having so many terrorist activities not  only in our country but all over 
the world? We don't have the sense of universal brotherhood. So, it is 
very, very necessary that we have to inculcate in our children some of 
these qualities like honesty, integrity, love for humanity, peace and 
non violence. The Father of the Nation, as all of us know, Mahatma 
Gandhi, fought for the independence of the nation, by only using non-
violence as his weapon, and he succeeded. That should serve as a 
great model for all of us. According to the value-based education of 
Satya Sai, the empahsis has to be on development and self-
realization, which means self-knowl edge, self-control, self-discipline 
and self-sacrifice. 
When we turn around, we see that most of us seem to be self-
centred, and this self-centred attit ude or character really leads to 
corruption, nepotism. Of that, we see a large amount in our country 
now. Maybe, when I say so, I am confining myself to our nation. 
Devotion and dedication to our profession is missing a lot. If you think 
of higher education-l have been in the field of higher education for a 
long time, we started my career as a lecturer with seventy-five rupees 
plus twenty-five rupees as dearness allowance; we were very happy. 
We were able to do 30 hours of work, even 35 hours of work per 
week; we never grumbled. Today, I am not envious of the salary that 
has been given to the university teachers and the college teachers by 
the UGC or the State Government or the Central Government or the 
Central University, but if you meas ure the amount of work that has 
been put in, the amount of work quantit atively as well as qualitatively, 
I do not know whether the salary that has been paid is proportionate 
to the work that is being done. 
Another thing that I feel important, in addition to dedication 
and devotion, is that the people shoul d be devoid of discrimination of 
humanity in terms of caste, cree d, community, language and religion. 
But instead of that, the discrimination between right and wrong, who 
should say that ft is right or wrong? Your own conscience. Self-
conscience should be developed through education to our children. 
There is so much of egoism. Humility has to be developed. 
But my own experience is that humility is mistaken for your weakness. 
But it should not be. Of course , everybody should be appreciating 
humility in an individual. So, the total personality of an individual 
should be developed. For that, physical, emotional, intellectual and 
spiritual values should be 
253

RAJYA SABHA       [29 November, 2001] 
inculcated. That is the total perso nality. Psychologis ts like Peashe, 
Erik Enkson in those days talked about personality development, 
emphasising on the sense of independence. Many of our people, 
either at home or in school, do not promote the sense of 
independence in our children. Spo onfeeding: they are dependent too 
much on the parents. Today, you see the bag's load that they bring 
from the schools. Who does the homework? The mother does the 
homework. So, we are not allowing our children even in the learning 
stage to be independent. The sense of industriousness is lacking a lot 
in our country. We do not believe in hard work at all. The sense of 
industriousness, the sense of achievement and the sense of integrity-- 
these are all things that the great psychologists thought of in those 
days. Today, the great philosophers and educationists also strongly 
demonstrate that education should culminate in service to the society. 
The growing concern over the erosion of essential values and 
the problems that the society is facing such as terrorism and 
communal riots-tnat is one of the Resolutions that will come up next-
corruption, nepotism in the society, breakdown of the families-that we 
are seeing a lot in our Indian society today-has brought to focus the 
need for a value-oriented education. I think, we have to prepare at 
least the next generation through education, the value-oriented 
education. It is, after all, the future  generation and the future citizens 
who are to build the nation from bad to good, good to better, better to 
the best. ...(Interruptions)... Sir, I will take a few minutes more. 
The Parliamentary Standing Committee on Human Resource 
Development in its Report of 1999 on value-based education has 
said: 
"Education should aim at multi-faceted development of a 
human being-his intellectual, physical, spiritual and ethical 
development. In order to preserve, maintain and advance the 
position of our country in the worl d, it is imperative that there 
should be a comprehensive programme of value-oriented 
education, starting from the pre-primary level, embracing the 
entire spectrum of educational process." 
"The minds, the heads, the hearts and the hands of the 
children are to be engaged in forming their own character to know 
what is good, love good and do good". Truth, satya, dharma, prema, 
shanti and ahimsa are the five core universal values on which value-
based education could be built. The world over, it is acknowledged 
that the ultimate goal of education is to build the belief and faith in the 
young children, even before they start 
254 

[29 November, 2001]      RAJYA SABHA 
their schooling, that every child or every human being has a divine 
spirit within. Once we think in terms of self-realisation, naturally, it will 
direct itself towards God realisation. I am not talking of high 
philosophy. Today, a young child, a four-year old child, who sits 
before a computer, can make anything on the earth. If you try to put 
this kind of education in his mind, I am sure, he will easily accept it. 
You can do it through the computer . He will enjoy it, accept it and 
learn it better. We can do this, through meditation and through yoga 
classes. The Ramakrishna Mission is running a number of institutions. 
We can bring it as a moral value itself. Sri Satya Saibaba institutions 
conduct some awareness course all over the world. That awareness 
course can be accepted by any religion and any society in any part of 
the world. 
In conclusion, I would like to say that education is not the 
personal property of any single individual. It is the property of 
everybody in our country, in the world; it does not belong to any 
group. The revision of curriculum is necessary because a long period 
has elapsed since we got it revised. But, when the revision is done, all 
the concerned agencies should be consulted and it should be properly 
implemented.  Thank you.
